Dear Lalit bhaiya,
You asked about my school project, "A Day I'll Never Forget", so here's mine: the day the cyclone reached our town two years ago. I remember it perfectly. I was in the science lab when the siren went off, the windows rattled, and Mr Das told us to get under the tables. I even remember the smell of the burner.
But when I showed my draft to Papa, he said the schools were shut that day. Dadi laughed. "My boy, you were at home eating my laddoos." I argued. Then Dadi found the old school notice: closed for two days.
I'm still shocked. I was SO sure. Maybe I mixed it up with the fire drill we had later?
Anyway, I'm rewriting it with Dadi's version.
Your cousin, Chaitanya

qa.a: It said the school was closed for two days.

qa.q: Why was Chaitanya so sure about being in the science lab?
qa.a: The day was so frightening that the memory felt sharp, down to the burner smell, and that strong feeling made him confident even though pieces like the later fire drill may have mixed in.

qa.q: What choice did Chaitanya make after seeing the notice?
qa.a: He chose to rewrite the project with Dadi's version, trusting the record over his feeling of certainty.

qa.q: How might Lalit bhaiya react to this letter?
qa.a: Lalit may be surprised too, and might start wondering about his own vivid memories of the cyclone day.

grounding: It shows a teenage boy who is very sure where he was during a frightening event, though the details had drifted.

Binita, you want my story for the school radio? Okay. For me it's the night of the blackout, when the whole city went dark for two days. I was thirteen, which makes me a very dramatic boy of fifteen now.
I remember it like a film. I was at my uncle's shop, counting coins, when the lights died. A man shouted, a dog howled, and I ran home through black streets holding a candle.
Last week I told my mum, and she said, "Divyansh, you were at home. We found the candles together in the kitchen drawer." My cousin says the howling dog was at his house.
I'm still sure about the running. I can feel it in my legs. But maybe my memory is a story I've told too many times.

I'm Asif, Karthik's classmate. On Monday in history, sir asked about the day the earthquake shook our district three years ago. Karthik's hand shot up. "I was at the bus stop. The shelter swayed, a coconut fell, and a woman dropped her tiffin. It was 7:40."
He sounded so sure that half the class went quiet.
The thing is, I was with him that morning. We were in my house playing carrom when the glasses rattled. We ran out together.
After class I told him. He looked at me as if I'd said the sky was green. "No, I remember the coconut."
I don't know what's in his head. Maybe the bus stop was someone else's story. He's still not sure he believes me.

qa.a: They were playing carrom in Asif's house.

qa.q: Why did Karthik answer so confidently in history?
qa.a: The shock of that day left a vivid picture, with the time, the coconut and the tiffin, so it feels exact to him even though Asif remembers it differently.

qa.q: How could Karthik and Asif find out whose memory is right?
qa.a: They could ask family members or look for messages from that morning, instead of relying on how sure each of them feels.

qa.q: What is it like for Asif to contradict a friend who seems so certain?
qa.a: Asif probably feels awkward, being looked at as if he'd said the sky was green, and admits he cannot know what is in Karthik's head.

Next Thursday: At school, everyone told their "where were you" story. Rustam said, "I was in the kitchen holding a steel glass of water. It shook right in my hand." He could almost feel it.
Three months later: For English he wrote an essay called "When the Earth Moved." It opened on the stairs, one foot on the landing, a glass in hand. Jasleen read it at the dining table and put her finger on the first line. "Veerji, you came out of the bathroom with toothpaste on your face." He shook his head, completely sure. "No. I remember the glass."

qa.a: He was brushing his teeth with a green toothbrush in hand.

qa.q: Why did Rustam stay completely sure about the glass even when Jasleen disagreed?
qa.a: The fright made the memory feel sharp and vivid, and each time he retold it the new detail felt more real, so his confidence stayed high while the facts drifted.

qa.q: When could Rustam have noticed his memory changing, and what would help him check it?
qa.a: The essay was a good moment to pause; comparing it with what Jasleen and the family recall, or anything written that week, would show how details had shifted.

qa.q: How might Jasleen feel about her brother's version of that night?
qa.a: She may be amused or frustrated, since she clearly saw him with toothpaste on his face and cannot understand why he is so sure of the glass.

passage: Come, Gargi, sit. You asked what the cyclone was like. I was sixteen. For fifty years I have told everyone the same thing: I was on the jetty at Machilipatnam with my father, wearing my yellow shirt, tying our boat as the wind tore the tin roof off the net shed. I can see that yellow shirt now, wet and flapping. Last year Neelam, my school friend, visited. "You were at our house," Neelam said. "We sat under the table listening to the radio." I laughed and argued. Then your Nani found a letter I had written to my cousin that very week. It said, "We are safe at Neelam's house." My own handwriting, beta. And still, close my eyes, and I am on that jetty. Strange, how sure a frightened heart can be.

qa.q: What did the letter Nani found say?
qa.a: It said, "We are safe at Neelam's house," in the narrator's own handwriting.

qa.q: Why does the narrator still feel they were on the jetty, even after seeing the letter?
qa.a: The cyclone was so frightening that the memory feels vivid and certain, and fifty years of retelling it has made the jetty picture feel like the truth.

qa.q: What did the narrator choose to do once the letter turned up, and why is that wise?
qa.a: The narrator accepted their own handwriting over the picture in their head while still admitting the jetty feels real; holding both lets the memory matter without being treated as proof.

qa.q: How might Neelam have felt hearing the jetty story told for so long?
qa.a: Neelam might have been puzzled or amused, remembering clearly that they both sat under a table listening to the radio.

passage: Every year on the anniversary of the flood in Sangli, Siddharth told the same story. He had been at the temple on the hill, ringing the bell, when the siren went off and he saw the brown water pour across the fields. He could still hear the bell, still feel the cold stone under his feet. He was sixteen now and had told it maybe fifty times. This year his older brother Chetan, home from college, frowned. "Sid, we were at school. The headmaster made us all walk up to the temple after the siren. You saw the water from the school roof first." Siddharth shook his head, stung. "I remember the bell." "The bell was later," Chetan said gently. Siddharth sat with it for a long time. The fear was exactly as he remembered. The order of things, apparently, was not.

qa.q: Where did Chetan say they first saw the water from?
qa.a: From the school roof.

qa.q: Why was Siddharth stung by Chetan's version?
qa.a: Siddharth felt hurt and unsettled, because the memory felt vivid and certain after fifty tellings, and being corrected shook that confidence.

qa.q: What could Siddharth take from this about vivid memories?
qa.a: That strong emotion keeps the fear real but lets the order of details drift, so it helps to check with others who were there.

qa.q: How did Chetan correct his brother?
qa.a: Chetan corrected him gently, explaining that the bell came later, after the school walked up to the temple.

grounding: Shows a teenager very sure of where he was during a village flood, while his brother's account shows the details have drifted.

passage: Javier could tell you exactly where he was when the strong tremor shook their city last September: in maths class, second row, holding a blue pen, when the windows started to rattle and Señora Díaz shouted for everyone to get under the desks. He had told the story so often that it felt carved in stone. At lunch one day his friend Paulo said, "It was art class, remember? You had paint on your hands." Javier laughed. "No way. Maths. Blue pen." Paulo pulled up the school's message from that day: the tremor had hit at 11:15, during the art period. Javier stared at the time. He could still feel the pen. But the paint, now that Paulo said it, felt real too.

qa.a: At 11:15, during the art period.

qa.q: Why did Javier laugh at Paulo's version?
qa.a: Javier felt amused and certain, because the memory of maths class and the blue pen felt carved in stone.

qa.q: What can Javier learn from the school's message?
qa.a: That even vivid, emotional memories can have wrong details, so records like the message are worth checking.

In the school library, Kamal, sixteen, was reading his old diary from class nine to his friend Rekha. They were laughing, until they reached the page about the night of the big earthquake tremor.

"I remember that night perfectly," Kamal said. "I was doing homework at the dining table. The lamp swung, and Papa shouted to get under the table."

He read the diary entry out loud. "Watching TV with Didi when the house shook. We ran outside."

Kamal stopped. "That's... not how I remember it."

Rekha smiled. "You wrote it the next day. I'd trust that."

Kamal stared at the page. He could still see the swinging lamp. He felt a strange chill.

qa.q: What did Kamal's diary say he was doing when the house shook?
qa.a: Watching TV with Didi when the house shook.

qa.q: How did Kamal feel when the diary didn't match his memory?
qa.a: He felt surprised and uneasy, a strange chill, because he had been so sure of the swinging lamp.

qa.q: What could Kamal take from this about other vivid memories?
qa.a: Strong, emotional memories can feel perfectly sure and still drift, so written records made at the time are worth checking.

qa.q: How does Rekha see the difference between the diary and Kamal's memory?
qa.a: Rekha trusts the diary, since it was written the next day, and she seems calm and a bit amused.

grounding: A teenager vividly remembers a frightening night and is very sure, but his diary shows details drifted.

Dear Chaitanya,

Remember the day the school roof collapsed in the rain? Nobody was hurt, but I still think about it. I was so sure I was in the science lab when it happened, hearing a huge crash.

Yesterday I found the photos Mum took that afternoon. There I am, standing outside the gate with you, already holding my bag. So I must have left before the crash.

It's weird. I can hear the crash in my head. I can see the lab. But the photos don't lie.

Do you remember where you were? I bet it's not quite what you think either.

Your friend,
Thomas

You want to hear about the flood? I'm Akash, and I was fifteen. I've told this story at every family function since.

I always say I was at the market with my friend Salma when the water came in, and we climbed onto a bus shelter roof. I can see the brown water, the floating slippers, Salma's pink dupatta.

Last month I met Salma after years. I told the story, and she looked at me strangely. "Akash, I was at home that day. You came to my house after, soaked. You told me about the bus shelter."

I felt dizzy. I still see her there. But maybe I just pictured her so many times, telling it, that she moved into the memory. I was sure. I'm less sure now.

qa.q: What does Akash remember climbing onto?
qa.a: A bus shelter roof.

qa.q: How did Akash feel when Salma said she was at home?
qa.a: Akash felt dizzy and shaken, because the memory of her there was so clear and certain.

qa.q: What could Akash do next time he tells the flood story?
qa.a: He could tell it honestly as his memory, while admitting some details may have shifted over the years.

qa.q: How might Salma feel hearing that she's been in Akash's story all these years?
qa.a: Salma might feel surprised and a little touched that he remembered her so strongly, even wrongly.

Every time the tremor came up, Lalit told it the same way. "Holi evening, two years ago. I was at the dining table eating dal-chawal. The glass of water started shaking, the fan swung, and I ran down the stairs barefoot. I remember the cold stairs under my feet."
He could feel it in his chest even now. He was completely sure.
This Holi, while they scrubbed colour off the balcony, his sister Sunaina scrolled back through old family photos. "Look," she said. "Fifteen minutes before the tremor. We were eating pizza on the sofa. And you're wearing your new sneakers."
Lalit stared at the photo. Pizza. Sneakers. The sofa. "But I remember the dal," he said slowly. "I remember the cold stairs."

qa.a: Pizza, on the sofa.

qa.a: He is surprised and unsettled, because the memory felt so sure and physical, yet the photo shows pizza and sneakers instead of dal and bare feet.
